Outbreak of Respiratory Illness Disrupts Ecuador’s Construction Materials Sector

QUITO, June 21 — A respiratory illness outbreak among workers in Ecuador’s construction materials industry is causing significant disruption, company officials and union representatives said Friday, with several major sites reporting reduced output and temporary shutdowns.

The outbreak, which began earlier this month, has affected both quarry and cement production sites across multiple provinces, including facilities operated by Holcim Ecuador SA. Industry sources report that dozens of workers have been hospitalized with acute respiratory symptoms, while hundreds more have been instructed to isolate at home pending medical clearance.

“In the past week, our company has seen a reduction in workforce availability by nearly 30 percent,” said Andrea Gómez, spokesperson for Holcim Ecuador SA. “We are prioritizing employee health and safety, and have implemented enhanced health protocols, but the impact on production is unavoidable at this stage.”

The National Construction Materials Association (ANMAC), which represents industry firms, estimates that output across the sector has dropped by at least 25 percent since the outbreak began. “Some plants are operating with skeleton crews or have paused certain lines altogether,” said ANMAC president Santiago Vélez, warning that if the situation continues, supply shortfalls could affect ongoing construction projects in the coming weeks.

At a major concrete block facility operated by Productos Andinos, an estimated 45 out of 120 workers are currently absent due to illness or quarantine. Plant manager Luis Ruiz described the situation as “unprecedented in recent memory,” noting that daily shipments have fallen to half their usual volume. “We are in close contact with health authorities and doing everything possible to support our employees,” Ruiz said.

The Ministry of Public Health has dispatched medical teams to several affected sites to conduct testing and contact tracing. “We are working closely with company management to contain the outbreak and ensure proper care for those affected,” said Dr. Carla Espinoza, regional health coordinator for Pichincha province.

Unions are urging companies to guarantee paid sick leave, provide personal protective equipment, and stagger shifts to reduce further transmission. “Many workers are anxious about job security and their families’ well-being,” said union leader Mario Cedeño. “Our priority is to ensure no one is forced to choose between their health and their livelihood.”

Authorities have not confirmed the precise cause of the illness, and investigations remain ongoing. Industry leaders say they are closely monitoring the situation and preparing contingency plans should the outbreak persist into July.
